thereby clarifying that the lives of all sentient beings are of great importance.
Mencius praised the striking of the bell at its consecration,
knowing that the King’s virtue had moved away from killing.
The former kings comforted the coarse and rescued those in urgent distress.
Therefore, although his benevolence is profound, he does not abruptly impose harsh prohibitions.
The Tathāgata has exhausted the depths of spiritual intelligence and reached its ultimate limit;
thus, he regards with equal gravity the lives of beings across the five realms of existence.
Abstaining from killing is the foremost of all precepts.
King Bimbisāra received retribution for his actions regarding the white hare;
the Śākya clan suffered extinction because of the yellow fish.
This is to demonstrate the principle of retribution;
all of it is profound and subtle,
circuitous yet not obscure.
If, upon rebirth, one is able to hear the Way and reverently practice the precepts of the Dharma,
then one will certainly not fall into the vast plains or suffer in the pits of Mafusai.
And even when already fallen, [one may still be saved].
If one has faith in the Dharma and can penetrate it thoroughly, one will certainly transcend the present difficulties.
Even if the karmic offenses from the past were heavy such that there is a prior retribution,
once the virtue of the precepts is subsequently attained, one will certainly not encounter such a pit in a future life.
What is called "dispensing divine power upon those in dire straits" and thereby "rescuing lives from grievous injustice" follows this very path.
How supreme is compassion!
Now, though one may possess worldly excellence, if they lack the mind of the Way,
they will violate and harm the lives of many in order to seek retribution for their own oppression.
This is logically correct.
The Buddha abides in principle and employs the Dharma to save sentient beings; if one does not follow the Dharma, then principle cannot provide horizontal salvation.
How could it be that the Buddha lacks reality?
It is like Bian Que:
if one treats an illness with medicine yet does not trust it or take it,
and the illness is not cured, is it because Bian Que was not skillful?
Geng Gong of Luyang was a distant descendant of the Jiugang clan;
that he was able to turn back the sun, cause springs to gush forth,
and cause insects and tigers to flee before his virtue was entirely due to his manifest sincerity moving all things.
The resonance of the Way of the Gods is precisely the resonance of the Buddha.
Had they been in Qin or Zhao, they certainly would not have fallen into such peril;
thus, those who did fall were all lacking in sincerity.
By what means did they come to move the Buddha so that he melted away their records? Indeed,
with a multitude capable of communicating with the divine,
they gathered in the hall where transformation reaches its ultimate limit.
Therefore, Mount Sumeru can indeed be seen within a mustard seed.
Furthermore, although tigers and pigeons exist now, they may have been human beings in the past;
there has always been the possibility for such karmic conditions to meet.
Thus, encountering the auspicious fortune of meeting a Buddha,
she cast herself into the water to save him and cut her own thigh to substitute for his life.
Had it not been for a profound resonance capable of moving heaven, how could one have repaid such slaughter with one's own life?
Regarding the task of melting and refining [the mind], how could one dare to act recklessly? When the myriad things die, they all return to their own nature; how then can one doubt the Buddha?
Indeed, such is the intensity of his resolve.
Thus, by contemplating them, one sees;
by addressing them, one hears.

By extending this principle, we see that Zhou and Kong dreamed of Yao and Shun, and though they sought the reality of their forms, the distance between ancient and modern times was vast, and the remoteness of the Fuyan Mountains was immense; yet, their profound communion remained unimpeded. Therefore, one can believe that through pure contemplation and the power of responsive resonance, one may behold the Buddha of Infinite Life, transcending hundreds of billions of worlds and arriving there without effort.
Why do you say that the Great Emptiness has no distinctions?
Now, the Way lies in refining the spirit and does not depend on preserving the physical form.
Therefore, śramaṇas consecrate their bodies by burning them, sharpening the spirit and severing worldly attachments.
The spirit cannot be extinguished, yet it can hasten toward its destination;
how could there be any burden?
One is bound by the constraints of human relations and navigates the rugged terrain of the six sensory passions.
What have you gained from me that you seek to burden the divine?

If you truly sever [worldly ties], then day by day you will diminish what is turbid and gradually advance toward the Way. Yet, through arduous effort for the sake of glorious sights, you exhaust your resources to dwell in remote seclusion; before long, such things vanish, and suddenly the person perishes. What name and reality one acquires does not exceed that of a thief who usurps another’s place. To construct a hall to house the spirit is to make it profound and solemn in its mystery.
When the form follows its subtlety, the spirit departs with it to the distance.
When subtle, the response is pure; when distant, the blessing is wondrous.
Between one who steals across and the Way, which is superior?
Suddenly seizing that which enables one’s transcendence in the prime of life,
their hidden practice accords with the divine spirit,
and their merit and virtue manifest in subsequent incarnations.
How could one possibly perceive what they have attained?
Now, human affairs are in motion and must penetrate the Way of the Spirit; nothing occurs without cause, for it must necessarily arise from a reason.
If the retribution of the unseen world were not as previously argued, [then all would be in vain].
Then by what principle would six hundred thousand lives be buried in a pit?
Since one must repay those who have buried them in a pit,
one must surely also repay those who have not.
Now, among the men of the Warring States,
there were those as subtle as Anqi Sheng and as reclusive as the Four Sages of Mount Hongluo;
they possessed dragon-like countenances yet ruled empires, and their domains were as vast as the earth.
Their illustrious reputations and abundant achievements are beyond counting; yet,
while all were within the range of Houyi’s bow,
why was it that only this one person remained so?
Is it not the case that each [result] is what corresponds to one's prior retribution?
Since we see that blessings are accomplished through past deeds,
it is clear that present actions will not fail to bear fruit for future lives.
Since we see that the superior and inferior ranks in this world are already distinguished by one's past lives,
how could there possibly be any confusion regarding what one shall receive after death?
This is the intent of the sutras.
They say that when they encountered the Buddha’s transformative manifestation,
it was entirely due to their long-standing accumulation of auspicious merit; thus,
their encounter with him was as it was.
Now, there has never been even a moment of response;
all such faults lie in the absence of conditions.
Yet you, on the contrary, falsely accuse the ultimate Dharma of being a fabrication.
Alas! The divine inspection is most manifest.
The calamity of insulting the sages is truly to be feared.
I venture to ask:
as for this "empty construction," does it belong to the sage, the worthy person, or the petty person?
Now, the sage has no fixed mind.
It is simply a matter of following the nature of things so that they may reach their full development.
If the body perishes and the spirit is extinguished,

What more could there be?
They deceive them by claiming there is no extinction and mislead them with the promise of attaining Buddhahood,
causing them to burn their hair and beard, scar their skin, and sever the flesh of their bodies.
The number of their descendants who have been suppressed is immeasurable.

including Jīvaka and Gandhāra, and others.

indeed, from Nāgārjuna onwards...

Thus, is the matter of the Yellow-Faced Master not perfectly clear?

this too is a testimony borne by the Way.

his traces and deeds were so clearly manifest that their transformative influence spread far and wide.

The fourfold assembly undergoes suffering until death without regret.
If the principles were deceptive and obscure, and the events not truly extraordinary,
how could they have been willing to sacrifice themselves and shatter their desires to honor that which has no form?

If the substance of a shadow is non-existent and yet sounds emerge from it as it moves back and forth, then why is it that those who have come from antiquity to the present exert themselves in asceticism and renounce desire? The treatise says:
Now, the reason why the Way of Governance has been clarified and manifested since antiquity is that it intends to preserve life.

Therefore, the Buddhas awaken them to it and guide them toward non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Non-arising cannot be realized instantaneously, so they lead [beings] there by stages.
Since the good and evil of birth are identical,
if one ascends ever higher through the rewards of goodness, then the state of ultimate clarity can be reached step by step.
Therefore, its Way is as vast as the deep blue sea.
There is nothing small that it does not permeate, and nothing great that it does not penetrate.
Although those who dwell far away from worldly affairs and prioritize the preservation of life may seem remote,
they nonetheless remain firmly molded by the gradual influence of the Five Classics and are encouraged and assisted by the teachings of ritual and morality.
The reason people of the present age treat blessings and calamities with contempt regarding the Way of Heaven is much like that of Sima Qian,
who was moved by the example of Boyi and lamented his fate.
Indeed, how could the Sage Confucius have spoken falsely?

yet Yan Hui and Ran Geng met with early death and illness, and nothing was heard of their descendants,

All such cases as these are logically untenable.
Yet how could there be any principle that is not universally applicable?
Thus, the doctrine that one receives blessings in this life but suffers calamity in the next through the three miserable realms is [untenable].
One cannot help but believe this.

Thus, the teachings of Confucius rely upon those of the Śākya clan to achieve full understanding.
Can this not be called the profound, ultimate, and unchanging Way?
Now, human affairs are as fleeting and chaotic as drifting clouds; existence and extinction are like illusions.
Encompassed within a hundred years, there is no one—from the infant to the aged—who does not come to an end.
This holds true even for those with yellowing hair and wrinkled backs.
One still feels that what has passed was but a fleeting moment;
how much more so for those durations that are shorter?
Moreover, time never ceases and its movement is inexhaustible.
Throughout countless and boundless kalpas in the past,
I have read and reviewed [this] one by one until the present day.
Now, having accumulated these moments of reading up to a hundred years, [the time has come].
How could it be difficult to reach [such a state], yet few are able to achieve even half of it?
Indeed, among things that charm the dew-laden body of the morning,
there is generally no substance of pure transcendence.
Why do you wallow in the stench of decay for a mere moment,
thereby obstructing the long-enduring spirit,
and fail to distance yourself from the winds of the distant past?
Although they are called the families that assist the Dharma in governing the world,
how could they alone be without a share in the Great Way?
It is only that they meander within the realm of humanity and are clamorous upon the worldly path.
Therefore, it is only the human path that is considered flourishing,
while the divine realm is regarded as utterly insignificant.
If one were to turn back from the wilderness of the human world and ascend the mountain peaks, [one would find the divine].
Gazing afar with wondrous vision,
one beholds the vastness of the heavens and the earth’s pure clarity,
and the marvels of the sun and moon shining through with penetrating brilliance.
How could it be that there is no presence of the majestic and solemn spiritual power of the successive sages within it?
Is it merely a place where crowds of people disperse and worldly affairs are hurriedly pursued?
Surely, one must cherish the distant in order to open the mind’s contemplation of the Way of the Spirits.
One perceives the resonance of the spiritual numen through its manifest clarity and stillness.
In ancient times, Zhongni (Confucius) cultivated the Five Classics in Lu to transform the world.
When he reached the remote heights of Mount Taimeng,
the world and the state of Lu both appeared small by comparison;
was this not because his spirit merged with the eight directions of space, thereby transcending the mundane age?
Thus, the composition of the Five Classics was merely a response to their minor aspects within a brief moment.
How can the world then use them to obstruct the Buddha-dharma and refuse to believe it?
I ask: regarding those who do not believe now, do you mean that there are no spirits or deities whatsoever outside of the common people?
Or do you mean that such beings exist, yet simply that there is no Buddha?
If there were no spiritual deities at all and only human beings existed,
then who would have commanded the dark bird to descend and give birth to the Shang dynasty?
And who would have left behind the giant footprint to move the spirits and give birth to Qi (the future Fuxi)?
Since the Han, Wei, Jin, and Song dynasties all received auspicious mandates,
we know that beyond the reach of sight and hearing,
the Way of the Spirit is brilliantly manifest.
That which possesses spiritual principle must necessarily have a subtle ultimate; that which attains the One and becomes numinous—what else could it be than the Buddha?
As for this spirit, it responds mysteriously according to conditions, yet its responses do not pre-exist.
If one proceeds from reality to transformation, what concern is there that it will not be exhaustive?
Why must one employ deceptive objects before providing instruction?
Such, then, is the reality of its method.
The faith in its teaching cannot admit of doubt.
The treatise says:
All living beings take the spirit as their master;

therefore, even toward the numinous power of the ultimate mystery, they all possess a principle by which they may be moved. Thus, although Yao was far removed [in time], the hundred beasts danced in response to his virtue.
Is this not indeed a matter of resonance? Thus,
the Buddha is the sovereign of the myriad resonances,
as are the sun, moon, seas, and mountains.
There still exist the rituals of morning and evening,
as well as the principles of ancestral offerings and regional sacrifices;
how much more so for the community of the Buddha’s Way?
Those of superior capacity exhaust the mysteries beyond the realm of birth;
those of middling capacity receive bodies within the wondrous birth;
and those of inferior capacity escape the three miserable realms.
Now, the teachings propagated in this world aim to achieve governance within the span of a single lifetime.
Those who reach the profound mystery are few, while those who conform to worldly ways are many.
How could they not collectively align with and habituate themselves to worldly sentiments, asserting that when death occurs, the spirit is extinguished?
Therefore, they do not strive to loftily set their wills upon the pure and remote,
but instead spend much of their time cultivating their worldly emotions;
thus, the Way of the gentleman is rarely found among them.
If one examines this through the Buddha-dharma, then the body is not the self;
it is merely a temporary lodging for a single rest.
The spirit, however, is what constitutes my true self.

Vast and enduring without end—such is the manifestation of supreme virtue within oneself, which flows forth inexhaustibly. As for that which is beautiful within, it will gradually ascend in purity until it reaches its ultimate fulfillment; whereas that which is base and evil possesses a far-reaching path toward self-renewal.
One may rectify past errors and ascend to higher realms.

Therefore, throughout antiquity, among both the refined and the coarse, there have been those who purified themselves and harbored lofty aspirations, practicing with reverence in the present to serve as a model for future generations; such individuals who advanced toward supreme virtue are beyond counting.
This is the efficacy of the Buddha-dharma.
These are all things obstructed by the world but opened up by the Buddha.
Regarding their categories, is there not a vast, harmonious clarity and a wondrous, open path?
How could one neglect and fail to uphold it?
For when wind passes through heat, it becomes pervasive; when it moves through a forest, it is surely pure.
When water is stirred, it becomes turbid; yet when it encounters clear stones, it is surely bright.
The spirits depend on gain and loss, yet they also rely upon that which they are entrusted with.
That you do not believe in the Buddha-dharma now is not necessarily due to your inherent disposition;

rather, it is because your mental state is thus conditioned. If you were to set aside your mind from worldly objects and allow yourself to be reflected by the pure and subtle, [your perspective would change].
Thus, the principles of the Buddha can be clarified and all matters will be believed.

Should one not carefully cultivate this intention? Relying on this, one proceeds with faith; ultimately, one will surely master the divine way, and the ancestral legacy of a hundred generations may be fulfilled.
To eternally deliver both the hidden and the manifest is the height of filial piety;
for all sentient beings to be moistened by benevolence is the ultimate of kindness;
to concentrate the spirit in solitary wonder is the pinnacle of the Way.
Piercing through to clarity without obstruction, illumination reaches its ultimate limit.

To turn one's back on the tracks and lose the way,
stumbling along until one passes away forever and sinks eternally into the nine realms—
how can this not be a cause for sorrow?
If it were not so, why would the world suddenly give birth to sagely sages and yet continue to nurture the ignorant and base?
From the Buddhas above down to the crawling insects below, how could this be?
All of these are manifestations of the gain and loss of the spirit.
Now, within the span of a person’s seven-foot physical body and several decades of life,
half is already consumed by sleep.
Furthermore, due to the many causes such as mourning and illness, one suffers even while the beauty and flourishing of the first half of life remain;
yet how long can honor, joy, and the fulfillment of one's ambitions last?
Moreover, the vigor of youth does not endure, and with a mind seeking glory, one fears disgrace.
Though they delight in the truth, they remain bound by sorrow and lack complete peace;
yet all vie with one another to enter the perilous paths of worldly convention,
while shunning the ascent upon the vast thoroughfare of the Buddha-dharma.
As for their wisdom: those in the world who,
failing to comprehend the root of conditions, remain perplexed by the principles of the Buddha,
are truly numerous.
Now, dependent origination is vast and boundless, beyond the reach of retrospective thought;
what it involves regarding loss and gain cannot be grasped through rational inquiry.
Because it lies beyond the six realms of the phenomenal world, the Buddha maintained it as something not to be discussed.
The preceding discourse has been completed;
I request that you further elaborate upon it by repeating its cycle.
Now, as for the Sage’s composition of the *Yī*:
Heaven hangs down its celestial signs;
through them, the divination of good fortune and misfortune, as well as order and chaos, can be known.
However, if one traces the nature of why things are as they are, there is nothing that the Sages did not clarify; thus, nothing remains unknown.
To now discard what can be known on account of what cannot be known is improper.
To act in opposition to the heavens by disregarding divination—
is there any such thing as not ceasing? One must not,
on account of an unclear beginning, turn one's back on the Buddha-dharma.
It is just like this.
Furthermore, because one does not recall the consciousness of a previous life,
it is claimed that the spirit did not previously exist.
Now, from the time a person is conceived in the womb until they reach childhood and adolescence,
it cannot be said that they lack spirit;
all this occurs within the span of a single lifetime— considering it from this perspective.
If one is already so oblivious as to have no recollection,
how much more so when passing through birth and death and experiencing different bodies?
How could past memories not cease?
What has been recollected has perished;
yet, since the constant presence of the spirit remains unimpaired, one does not fail to understand the beginning of conditions.
How could this hinder the principle from being eternally clear?
Zilu asked about death.
The Master said,
"While you do not yet know life, how can you know death?"
When asked about serving ghosts and spirits, he said, "I do not yet know how to serve men; how then can I know how to serve ghosts?
Was this not because You (Ran You) was exhaustive in his love for courage and sincere in his service to his ruler?
It is certainly appropriate that within a single lifetime one should inquire into the fundamental principles of birth, death, ghosts, and spirits,
even though such questions may seem trivial.
Since this is not a response to the fundamental principle of reality,
the teachings of the Buddha regarding human nature and the Way of Heaven cannot be heard.
Regarding the fourteen questions concerning whether sentient beings are finite or infinite,
the All-Knowing One set them aside and did not answer.
This was because answering them would be of no benefit and would lead instead to falling into evil and heterodox views.
Thus, those who receive the teachings of the sages and serve the Buddha ought surely to decline what is severed and partake of what is appropriate—
just as one who thirsts drinks from a river, drawing from its vast current to satisfy oneself.
Why must one seek the ultimate source on Mount Kunlun?
In all matters concerning the Buddha-dharma, if something contradicts the natural order of heaven,
it cannot be established in principle.
Thus, it may be appropriate to doubt them;
yet now there is no obstacle to their being possible,
and there is the actual fact of their conforming to Heaven and clarifying the spirit.
Is this not indeed true?
For when a person is born,
they are born together with sorrow.
Calamities and misfortunes arise from the events of the present age;
disasters and pestilences erupt from the realm of the obscure and hidden.
Though one may possess noble rank reaching to the clouds and command a host of a million followers, [it remains no avail].
At first, he was alone, sitting with his physical form and spirit awaiting impermanence;
yet while his family members were bustling about and his wife and children were playing joyfully,
he suddenly again sank into a state of dazed oblivion.
What reliance can ever be placed on human principles?
Since life passes like a crack in a wall, one ought to strive against slander and compete for longevity; yet people indulge their desires and commit excesses that bring harm.
Since the spirit is never extinguished, [one must act with caution].
Seeking to extinguish [suffering] yet failing to do so, one must again undergo rebirth due to the burden of transgressions.
The current masses of reckless beings and the myriad kinds of insects and creatures are all vivid warnings from history.
To devise a plan for this, there is only one way:
to entrust one's sincerity to the Buddha, to entrust one's heart to the observance of the precepts, and thereby to support the spirit.
Thus, while alive one receives divine assistance, and at death one ascends to purity.
He ascends in purity without end and will surely become a Buddha.
Although the Buddha himself spoke thus, people treat him with contempt.
How can one judge that this man is superior to a Buddha?
If one cannot overcome it,
will one not fall into that evil and suffer its extreme torments forever?
Alas for those born into the bitter poisons of the six extremes of suffering!
Therefore, the world knows no end.
Among those we have heard of or seen who died while practicing with vigor,
the majority were those whose spirits and intentions remained settled even when facing imminent peril.
If one single-mindedly invokes Avalokiteśvara, there is no distress that will not be relieved;
this is precisely what is meant by the sign of receiving divine assistance while alive and ascending to purity after death.
Now, as for the sovereign of ten thousand chariots—
The ruler of a thousand chariots has no leisure for food even when the sun declines;
the myriad people rely upon him only within the scope of a single transformation.
How can one cause the spirit to flourish and reign over the myriad transformations?
Now, we rely on the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius to nourish the people,
and savor the Buddha-dharma to nourish the spirit.
Thus, while alive they are enlightened sovereigns, and after death they become enlightened spirits;
they reign eternally as kings.
How could the Tathāgata deceive us?

It is not that I advocate for the exorbitant construction of stupas and the lavish crafting of images to support monks who indulge in hollow pretenses; such things are what I mean by "wasting wealth and harming the people.
If one fails to examine the profound reality and instead observes only superficial defects, one will surely react with reckless contempt toward the Dharma.

Indeed, they revere the Way and trust in its teachings; awakening to impermanence and the emptiness of form and matter, they possess a compassionate heart and maintain an orderly transformation of society.
They do not, out of noble status or arrogance, lightly take the lives of living beings, nor do they allow the unworthy to fraudulently assume improper vestments.
Is this not the height of "the world returning to benevolence," achieved by guiding them with virtue and regulating them with ritual?
As for one in a state of leisure and ease,
or in the person of a rustic dweller by the fields and marshes,
what is there to be regretted?
Yet he did not save his own spirit. Formerly,
when the Venerable Huiyuan was purifying his practice at Mount Lu,
I went there to rest for fifty days.
His character was lofty, pure, and steadfast, and his mastery of the principles of the school was exquisite;
he was truly a distant descendant of that lineage.
His teacher, Dharma Master An, possessed spiritual virtues that were naturally extraordinary.
Wei Yu and the Bhikṣu both possessed a spirit of pure sincerity;
they were companions whose mutual rapport had long been harmonized with the Way before they subsequently dwelt in solitude upon the mountain.

Therefore, the transformation of the divine spirits is profound within the crags and forests; when they suddenly converse with me amidst the cliffs, trees, streams, and ravines, there is a mysterious presence that transcends words yet inspires solemnity in those who encounter it.
All such arguments are merely the Venerable Master’s interpretation based on the intent of the scriptures.

Indeed, those who excel at responding to circumstances used bird tracks to establish writing and exhausted the mysteries of the spirit; the praise of the common people from a single word of Tiying brought about the success of a hegemonial enterprise, and corporal punishments were abolished forever. There are indeed matters where a slight, fleeting stimulus ultimately leads to a transcendence that reaches the heavens.
Now, with these crude and vulgar words, I seek to stir his feelings;
though my life shall suddenly end,
who knows that this will not lead him to transcend and ascend?

Sun Chuo’s “Discourse on Illustrating the Way” (Yudao lun):

Master Zong Bing’s Reply to He Chengtian’s Letter Refuting the “Treatise on the White and the Black,” Part 4. Sun Chuo’s “Discourse on Illustrating the Way” (3). Sun Chuo’s “Discourse on Illustrating the Way”: There may be those who harbor doubts regarding the Ultimate Way.
He illustrated this by saying:
"Now, the six realms of existence are vast and remote, and the myriad species are numerous and abundant;
the thousand transformations and ten-thousand changes are a浑沌 (húnchùn) mass without discernible beginning."
Therefore, those with localized knowledge each expect only what they have seen;
creatures of the scales and shells do not understand the affairs of the highlands and plains.
The species of feathered creatures do not recognize the vastness of drifting currents;
those who find contentment within a small well marvel at the capacity of one who roams the deep ocean.
Those who soar to a height of several *ren* may doubt their power to reach the heavens,
yet they remain bound within the confines of worldly teachings.
Examining at length the traces left by the Duke of Zhou and Confucius,
I maintain that the ultimate virtue reached its limit with Yao and Shun,
and that the subtle words were exhausted in Laozi and the *I Ching*.
Where, then, shall we again behold the wondrous delight beyond the mundane world, that profound illumination within the dark? Alas!
How the ceremonial cap is cast aside among those who dwell in naked barbarism.
The *Shao* and *Xia* were abandoned because they were vulgar and crude;

13. Discourse on the Three Retributions (Master Yuan) (5). This discourse on the three retributions was composed by Master Yuan based on the scriptures to address the doubts of laypeople regarding the lack of visible evidence for the effects of good and evil.
Karma has three types of retribution:
first, retribution in the present life;
second, retribution in the next life.
The third is retribution in subsequent lives.
Retribution in the present life refers to when good or evil deeds initiated in this very body are experienced by that same body.
Retribution in the next life is experienced immediately in the following birth.
As for subsequent retribution, it may be experienced after two, three, a hundred, or a thousand lifetimes;
only then is it received.

In the past, Vimalakīrti internally traversed the sublime path, his merit manifesting outwardly through his deeds. He was a man of profound wisdom who, though dwelling within the secular world, remained detached from worldly affairs. His eloquence was vast and his spiritual power was immense; he was truly one who had transcended the mundane. Yet, even such a person as this could not avoid being entangled by the heterodox teachings of the barbarians. How much more so for those like us, who are but commoners? Furthermore, the Great Sage [the Buddha] appeared in the world to illuminate the darkness of ignorance. He manifested his body in the human realm to guide sentient beings. It was precisely because he was a human that he was able to save humanity. Had he been a deity, he would have remained aloof from the world, and how could he have reached out to transform the people? Thus, it is clear that the Way of the Buddha is fundamentally superior to that of the barbarians. Now, the Daoist Gu has composed the "Treatise on the Barbarians and the Chinese," claiming that the Way of the Buddha is merely a branch of the Daoist Way. This is a grave error. If the Buddha were indeed a branch of the Daoists, why did he not appear during the time of the Yellow Emperor or Yao and Shun? Why did he instead emerge only after the Zhou dynasty had declined? If the Buddha were a branch of the Daoists, he should have appeared when the Daoist Way was flourishing; yet, he appeared only when the Daoist Way had already waned. This proves that the Buddha is not a branch of the Daoists. Moreover, the Daoists claim that the Buddha is a transformation of Laozi. But Laozi was a man of the Zhou, while the Buddha appeared in the land of India. If they were one and the same, why did they differ so greatly in their customs and practices? Furthermore, the Buddha taught the cessation of desire and the eradication of afflictions, whereas Laozi spoke of the preservation of the self and the nourishment of the spirit. Their goals and methods are diametrically opposed. How can they be considered the same? Thus, we know that the Buddha is not a branch of the Daoists, nor is he a transformation of Laozi. The Buddha is the teacher of all Buddhas, the father of all sentient beings, and the sovereign of the three realms. His virtue is vast and his wisdom is profound; he is the peerless sage of the world. To equate him with the Daoists is to utterly misunderstand the source of the Dharma. Because it is profoundly still and immutable, it ultimately returns to the wondrous fruit. As the Sūtra says: "The mind is the direct cause, ultimately attaining the fruit of Buddhahood. Your servant Ji says: To speak briefly of the causes of Buddhahood, their meanings are twofold.
The first is called the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*);
the second is called the direct cause (*hetu-hetu*).
"Condition" refers to the myriad forms of goodness.
The "correct" refers to the spiritual consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Because the myriad virtues possess the power to assist its manifestation, it is called the "conditional cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*); the spiritual consciousness is its fundamental substance, and thus it is called the "direct cause" (*mūla-hetu*).
Since it is stated that one ultimately attains the fruit of Buddhahood, this clearly verifies the principle of non-interruption. Furthermore, it says:
"If ignorance is transformed, it becomes clarity.
Examining the meaning and principle of this sutra, they can be sought as follows.
What is this? Now, the mind is the basis of all function;
while the basis is one, its functions are diverse.
These diverse functions naturally undergo arising and ceasing.

"The nature of the single source does not shift. My subject Ji said: "To refine away the dust and filth of the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) so that its luminosity becomes manifest—this interchange between light and darkness is called 'transformation.
As for the phrase 'the one source,' it refers to that which is neither prior nor subsequent."
"This refers to the numinous intelligence of ignorance. My subject Ji said:
"Since the numinous intelligence is fundamentally dark, it takes ignorance as its cause. However, the designation 'ignorance' is not a term for the Great Void."
"Earth and stone are insentient; how could they be said to possess ignorance?
His minister Ji replied, "To distinguish between good and evil, nothing is known except by the mind; to clearly discern right from wrong, nothing is perceived except through wisdom."
Without emotion, nothing can be discerned;
because the Great Void is without emotion,
it does not distinguish between the ignorant and the wise.
Since earth and stone are insentient, how could they distinguish between delusion and awakening?

Thus we know that delusion and awakening exist only where there is mind; folly and wisdom reside only where there is consciousness. Since it is called "ignorance" (avidyā), the principle is already established therein. Therefore, one should know that while cognitive deliberation ought to be clear, the substance [of the self] cannot escape delusion.
Because one is deluded and lacks discernment, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*). My humble servant Ji says:
Clarity is the fundamental nature;
yet because one responds to and recognizes external defiled objects, one cannot internally avoid delusion. To be deluded and thus fail to understand is what is termed ignorance.
It is because of this that the name [of emptiness] is established;
how could its meaning be mere vacuity? Yet, within the substance of ignorance, there is arising and ceasing;
arising and ceasing are its diverse functions.
Wang Xingyi did not change his response, and his subordinate Ji said:
"Since its essence exists, its function must also exist;
to speak of the function while denying the essence is incorrect."
The essence is not the function;
the function has its arising and ceasing, whereas the essence is without birth or extinction. One fears that by observing the differences in the function, [one will fail to see the essence].

He then claimed that the mind perishes along with its objects. My subordinate Ji said: "The deluded are confused regarding its essence (*tǐ*) and function (*yòng*), and thus they do not cease their suspicions.
Why is this? For essence and function are neither separate nor identical; apart from essence, there is no function."
Therefore it is said:
"The meaning of function is not separate from substance.
Therefore it is said.
Failing to see that they are not separate while being deluded by their non-identity— being thus deluded regarding their non-identity—
one then claims that the mind perishes along with its objects; therefore, following "ignorance" (avidyā),
the term "ground-abiding" (ālaya-bhūmi) is added as a designation for it.
This reveals that ignorance is itself the divine spirit (*deva*), and the nature of the divine spirit does not undergo transition. Your servant Ji says:
Ignorance is bound to the ground of abiding (*ālayavijñāna*).
This is intended to refute their delusion regarding consciousness;
yet those who harbor such doubts have never understood it. How is this known?
For example, as when a previous mind commits a grave evil that constitutes an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*).
The subsequent arising of consciousness is non-perceptual and wondrously wholesome;
the principles of good and evil are vastly divergent,
and the distance between the preceding and succeeding states is exceedingly remote.
If these functions were not based on a single root, how could they continue in such a manner? My subject Ji said:
"Were there not a single root, these functions would have nothing upon which to rely;
it is only because those who are deluded see their similar succession as one that they perceive them thus."
Therefore, by citing great goodness, he refutes the delusion of their continuity. Thus we know that while prior evil is extinguished of its own accord, the deluded consciousness does not shift;
and though subsequent goodness arises, the darkened mind remains unchanged. Master Ji said:
It has never been impaired by good or evil, nor by arising or ceasing; thus the Sūtra says:
"If it coexists with afflictions and various fetters, it is called ignorance."
"If that which is conjoined with all wholesome dharmas is called 'illumination' (vidyā),
is this not because the nature of mind-consciousness is one, yet it differs according to conditions? The subject Ji replied:
If good and evil arise alternately, how can they be said to coexist?
Yet people constantly respond to these words while remaining perpetually confused about their meaning;
therefore, I cite this essential passage to clarify the delusions of the multitude. Thus we know that birth, cessation, and shifting change are the retributions for past causes.
"Good and evil alternate and arise within the present realm," my subject Ji said.
"Arising and ceasing are caused by fundamental karma; it is not the present realm that makes them so.
Good and evil arise in the present realm; it is not fundamental karma that causes them to be thus. Rather, the mind is their root."
It has never been otherwise. My subject Ji said:
"Although their functions differ, their substance is not different;
this is because the source of their function is uninterrupted."
The principle of attaining Buddhahood is clear;
since one undergoes transition and cessation according to conditions, it is evident that birth and death can be brought to an end. Your servant Ji says:
The clarity of attaining Buddhahood is due to supporting its fundamental basis;
that birth and death can be exhausted is due to its functional application.
If there were function without a basis, one would be extinguished rather than achieving enlightenment.
If [the spirit] were fundamentally non-existent and useless, then it would follow that there is nothing to be extinguished.
Preface to the Refutation of the "Discourse on the Extinction of the Spirit," composed by Fan Zizhen, my brother-in-law, who authored the "Discourse on the Extinction of the Spirit," Xiao Chen.
He claimed that there was no Buddha,
asserting that his own eloquence could crush the mouths of the multitude and that he could convert a thousand people every day;
yet in my mind, I still harbored doubts about this.
I merely wish to briefly resolve their doubts and inquire into what they have not yet understood;
for the discussion thus far has centered on the relationship between the physical form and the spirit.
What is being debated concerns the essential principle.
If the *Spring and Autumn Annals* prescribes filial sacrifices for ancestral temples,
this is because the sages established teachings through the divine way and instituted ritual to restrain the ignorant.
Du Bo drew his bow and Bo You donned his armor;
they both claimed that there are naturally strange creatures between heaven and earth,
and that it is not the case that dead people become ghosts.
If this were so, it would not be tenable.
When interrogated by means of the Odes and the Documents and compared with past events,
one can only conclude that [the distinction lies] between the physical form and the spirit.
Distinguishing their separation and union:
if one realizes that body and spirit are of one essence and that their existence and extinction are no different,
then Master Fan will rouse himself with vigor and martial energy, and his golden walls and moats will remain distant and secure.
If the spiritual essence and the physical substance diverge in their paths, such that one’s rise and fall are distinct,
then my victory over the enemy and the acquisition of the prize would constitute the completion of my task.
Furthermore, although I clearly acknowledge the existence of the Buddha, my realization of the Buddha is not the same as that of the common world.
I shall set forth my original intent and append it to the left of this treatise. 26.

*Shenmie Lun* (The Discourse on the Extinction of the Spirit), by Xiao Chen (IX). Regarding the "Questions and Answers on the Extinction of the Spirit," these are the words of the proponent and the opponent in the original treatise. As for the "Questioner," this refers to the one who poses the current inquiry. The question is as follows:
The disciple said: "You speak of the extinction of the spirit.
How do you know it is extinguished?
He replied:
The spirit is identical with the form;
the form is identical with the spirit.
Therefore, when the form exists, the spirit exists.
"When the form perishes, the spirit is extinguished.
He asked:
"As for the form..."
"Non-knowing" is the designation for the spirit;
"knowing" is the name for that which possesses consciousness.
Knowledge and ignorance differ in their actual manifestation;
it is logically impossible for the spirit and the physical form to be one and the same.
That the spirit and the form are identical is something we have never heard of.
The answer is:
The form is the substance of the spirit.
The spirit is the function of the form;
thus, the form corresponds to its substance.
The spirit speaks of its function;
form and spirit cannot be distinct from one another.
An objection is raised:
Now, if one argues that body and spirit constitute a single entity, there ought to be evidence of their inseparability;
yet you simply state that "spirit is identical to the body" and "the body is identical to the spirit," asserting that body and spirit cannot be distinct from one another.
This argument is without evidence and contradicts the established analogy.
You now rely on a dream to prove that the body and spirit cannot share the same substance;
yet when a person is asleep, their body is an insentient object.
Yet there is that which is seen;
this is what the spirit encounters during its excursions. The spirit does not exist in isolation;
it must necessarily rely upon physical forms and instruments.
It is just as a person who cannot remain exposed must have a dwelling;
however, the physical body is a substance of impurity and darkness,
while the dwelling is a place of concealment and obstruction.
When the spirit returns within the physical form, its consciousness becomes faint and obscure;
thus, what was seen is regarded as a dream.
When a person enters their chamber, their spirit is temporarily obstructed.
Therefore, what is considered clarity may actually be delusion.
Suppose a person dreams of ascending into the profound void or traveling ten thousand li away:
is this not movement by means of the spirit, or else the movement of the physical form?
Since the form does not go away and the spirit does not depart,
how could this be possible?
If you claim that this is what is seen through mental construction (*saṃjñā*), [then...]
When one sleeps peacefully, the body is like a withered log and the breath is like cold ashes;
calling out, there is no response, and stroking it, there is no sensation.
If one then says that the spirit and the form are identical, it implies that both the internal and the external are equally exhausted.
Since external sounds and voices are no longer received,
how could internal thoughts and reflections arise? Thus,
it can be clearly understood that while the body is at rest, the spirit is already racing away.
Furthermore, there is doubt regarding all that is dreamed;
for instance, Zhao Jianzi’s dream was reversed and met with deceptive fortune,
while the dream of a naked boy singing "Ke Wu" resulted in entering Zou.
The dream of the minor official of Jin, who dreamed he carried his lord up to heaven and carried him out from the latrine, is an example of this; it was something that reason could not tolerate.
Lü Yi dreamed that he shot an arrow and hit the moon.
The dream of Empress Wu,
in which her intestines emerged and wound around the Chang Gate, is an example of this. Or, as when Lü Jiang perceived a portent before it had manifested,
she dreamed of heaven and named her son Yu.

The case of the people of Cao dreaming that a multitude of gentlemen were plotting to enfeoff them as lords is an instance of using metaphorical imagery; Cai Mao’s dream of losing a grain of rice resulting in the character for "official" (*zhí*) is another.

Wang Jun’s dream of three knives becoming a "state" (*zhōu*) is yet another example. Sometimes these dreams concern things that do not actually exist in reality, such as the Hu people’s dream of a boat.

The man of Yue who dreamed of riding [a dragon] is an example of this; sometimes it was verified and sometimes not. King Zhou of Yin dreamed of obtaining Fu Yue, while Emperor Wen of Han dreamed of finding Deng Tong—these were verifications.

Instances where it was not verified are numerous and need not be recorded in detail here. All of these involve a spiritual transformation so vast and obscure that the realms of the hidden and the manifest do not intersect.
One measures the *I Ching* to simplify the difficult and employs principle to examine what is not permitted;
the spirit’s wandering must necessarily be sought within the physical form.
Fearing that the latent numen might remain solitary and hidden within, one must ensure that it is not cut off from being beheld externally.
Although Dui may indeed support [his position] with the six types of dreams and provide it with the causal conditions of conceptualization,
logically this cannot be so.
He asks:
Being divine, it is not substantial;
being corporeal, it is not functional.
Since it cannot be categorized as either, where does its meaning reside?
Answer: The names differ, but the essence is one.
Question:
Since their names are already distinct,
how can their essence be one?
He replied:
The spirit in relation to the physical substance is like sharpness in relation to a blade;
the form in relation to its function is like a blade in relation to its sharpness.
The name "sharpness" is not the blade itself.
The name "sword" is not the sharpness itself.
Nevertheless, apart from sharpness there is no sword, and apart from a sword there is no sharpness.
It has never been heard that when a sword perishes, its sharpness remains.
"How could it be possible for the form to perish while the spirit remains?
The objection states:
"Now, a blade possesses sharpness because of the efficacy of whetting and sharpening."
Therefore, he was able to sever crocodiles and dragons in the water and cleave rhinoceroses and tigers on land;
yet when his resources were exhausted and his advantage spent, his sharp blades were inevitably blunted.
It transforms into a blunt edge;
thus, while the sharpness perishes, the blade remains.
This is precisely like the spirit departing while the physical form persists.
Why do you say that the sharpness and the blade are abandoned?
Are they not different in name but one in essence?
Since the blade and the sharpness do not perish together, [how can this be so?]
If form and spirit do not perish together,
then although one may draw an analogy from what is near, in reality the principle is contradictory.
[The opponent] asks:
The relationship between a blade and its sharpness, or as the Tathāgata has taught, between form and spirit—their meanings are not like this.
Why do I say so? It is because the substance of wood is devoid of consciousness.
Human nature possesses consciousness.
Humans possess a nature like that of wood,
yet they also possess a consciousness unlike that of wood.
"Is it not the case that the wood constitutes one [entity] while the person constitutes two?
He replied,
"How strange are these words!"
If a person possesses a physical form with a nature like that of wood,
yet possesses a consciousness like that of something other than wood as their spirit,
then one may engage in such a discussion as yours.
Now, the substance of a human being possesses consciousness;
the substance of wood lacks consciousness.
The substance of a human being is not the same as the substance of wood.
The substance of wood is not the substance of a person.
How could there be that which possesses the substance of wood and yet also possesses a consciousness distinct from that of wood?
Question:
That which distinguishes the substance of a human being from the substance of wood is simply that [the former] possesses cognition.
If a person lacks consciousness, how would they differ from wood?
He replied:
"A person does not possess a nature devoid of consciousness."
It is like wood, which has no form endowed with consciousness.
[The interlocutor] asks:
"Is not the physical remains of the deceased a substance devoid of consciousness?"
Answer: It is the substance of non-cognition.
Question:
"If that were so, then humans would indeed possess a substance like that of wood,
yet have a consciousness different from that of wood.
He replied:
The dead possess a substance like that of wood,
yet lack the consciousness of wood;
the living possess the consciousness of wood, yet differ from it.
Yet it lacks the substance of wood.
[The interlocutor] asks:
"Are not the bones and remains of the deceased the very same physical frame as that of the living?"
The answer is:
the form of the living is not the form of the dead;
the form of the dead is not the form of the living.
Since the regions have already been transformed,
how could there be the physical forms of living beings while possessing the skeletal remains of the dead?
Question:
If the physical form of the living person is not the skeletal remains of the dead person,
then the skeletal remains of the dead person should not have originated from the physical form of the living person.
If it does not arise from the physical form of a living being,
then from where do these bones and remains come?
He replied:
This is the transformation of the physical form of a living being into the skeletal remains of a dead one.
A question is asked:
Although the physical form of a living being transforms into the skeletal remains of a dead one, [how is this so?]
Is it not because there is death due to birth that we know the substance of death is the same as the substance of birth?
He replied:
For example, when a flourishing tree changes into a withered tree,
is the substance of the withered tree truly the same as the essence of the flourishing tree?
[The opponent] asks:
The flourishing body transforms into the withered body;
the withered body is itself the flourishing body.
It is like the substance of silk transforming into the substance of thread.
If the substance of the thread is identical to the substance of the silk, what fault is there?
He replied:
If withering were identical to flourishing,
and flourishing were identical to withering,
then flowers should fall during the time of flourishing, and fruit should form during the time of withering.
Furthermore, a flourishing tree should not transform into a withered tree,
because that which flourishes is itself the withered state;
once withered, there is nothing further to change.
Furthermore, since flourishing and withering are one and the same, why does it not wither first and flourish later?
Why must it necessarily flourish first and wither later?
Threads and fibers occurring simultaneously cannot serve as an analogy.
Question:
When the physical form of birth passes away, it should simply vanish into nothingness;
for what reason, then, does one continue to receive a physical form of death that persists through an unending succession?
The answer is:
This is because the essence of arising and ceasing necessarily possesses its own sequence.
Now, that which arises suddenly—
That which arises suddenly must perish suddenly;
that which arises gradually must perish gradually.
That which arises suddenly refers to the swift and impetuous;
that which arises gradually refers to the incremental.
This refers to the animate and the inanimate.
That there is both suddenness and gradualness is the principle of things.
An objection is raised:
The treatise says:
"The nature of man possesses cognition;
the nature of wood lacks cognition."
Is it not because humans perceive coolness and warmth and know pain and itching;
that they live when nourished and die when injured?
It is the same with trees:
they flourish in spring and wither in autumn.
If one plants it, it will surely grow; if one uproots it, it will surely die.
What is meant by "insentience"?
The physical substance of humans today is just like that of wood.
When the spirit remains, the form is established;
when the spirit departs, the form is discarded.
This establishment is precisely what constitutes the flourishing of the tree.
What has been discarded is simply withered wood.
How can you argue that this possesses spiritual cognition while claiming that the physical substance possesses cognition?
All things in the ten thousand phenomena know through spirit and not through substance;
they merely perceive the nature of growth and decay, and of life and death, like plants, trees, and insects.
The consciousness of living beings penetrates both security and peril, as well as benefit and harm.
Why would it not be so? Is it not the case that they possess a physical form like that of wood, yet also possess a cognitive awareness like that of wood which serves as their spirit?
In this case, form and spirit are two distinct entities that can be separated;
however, wood receives the partial influence of yin and yang,
whereas man contains the brilliant illumination of a singular spiritual essence.
Their consciousness may be the same,
yet their spirits are different.
This concerns the discourse on bones and physical frames, and the doctrine of the transmission of life and death.
Since the principle has already been settled and the matter has not undergone [such] experience,
what need is there for convoluted arguments?
Question:
If the body is identical to the spirit, then are the hands and other limbs also the spirit? Answer:
All these are portions of the spirit. Question:
If all these are portions of the spirit, then the spirit should be capable of deliberation.
The hands and other limbs should also be capable of deliberation.
[The opponent] replies:
The hands and other limbs possess the cognition of pain and itching.
Yet there is no concern regarding right or wrong.
A questioner asked:
"Are knowing and concern one and the same, or are they different?"
The answer is:
Knowing is itself deliberation;
when it is shallow, it is termed knowing.
If it is profound, it constitutes deliberation.
[The opponent] asks:
If that is so, there should then be two types of deliberation.
If thought already has two aspects, does the spirit have two as well?
The answer is: No.
The human body is singular;
how could the spirit be dual? Question:
If one does not attain these two [states], there is still the awareness of pain and pleasure, as well as the deliberation of right and wrong.
The answer is:
it is like hands and feet; though they are distinct, they together constitute a single person.
Although these sensations of pain and itching differ from one another,
they are nonetheless collectively comprised within a single spirit.
[The interlocutor] asks:
The deliberation regarding right and wrong does not involve the hands and feet.
With what, then, should it be concerned?
He replied:
The faculty of discerning right and wrong is that which presides over the organ of the mind.
A question is asked:
"Is this 'organ of the mind' the heart among the five viscera?"
The answer was:
"It is so. The questioner asked:
What distinction is there among the five viscera such that the mind alone possesses the capacity for deliberation regarding right and wrong?
The answer is:
The seven apertures are likewise no different;
why then is their function not distributed equally?
He asked:
Thought and reflection have no fixed direction.
How do we know that these are governed by the organ of the mind?
The answer is:
When the mind is diseased, thought becomes distorted;
therefore, we know that the mind is the root of deliberation. Question:
How do we know that it does not reside within the constituent parts of the eye and so forth?
The answer is:
if one considers that it might reside within the constituent parts of the eye.
Why does the eye not rely upon the auditory faculty?
[The opponent] asks:
Since the substance of deliberation (vitarka) has no inherent basis, it may rely upon the visual faculty.
The eye has its own fundamental basis;
it does not depend upon or borrow from other parts.
He replied:
Why is it that the eye has a basis while consciousness has no basis?
If consciousness had no basis within my physical form,
how could it be universally lodged in different locations?
Furthermore, one may project the sentiments of Zhang Jia onto the body of Wang Yi,
or [project] the nature of Li Bing [onto it].
"To rely upon the physical forms of Zhao and Ding— is this so? It is not so."
An objection states:
The treatise says that form and spirit are not distinct, and that the hands and other parts are all portions of the spirit.
This means that the spirit takes the body as its substance.
When the substance is complete, the spirit is complete;
when the substance is injured, the spirit is deficient.
What is the spirit?
It is consciousness and deliberation.
Now, some people may have their hands and feet severed or their skin and flesh mangled.
Yet their wisdom and thought remained undisturbed;
it was as when Sun Bin had his feet amputated and his military strategy became even more brilliant,
or when Lou Fu had his wrist severed and the Way of the Confucians finally found tranquility.
This spirit separates from the physical form;
this is a direct proof that when the body is injured, the spirit is not harmed.
However, the spirit employs wisdom to govern external things.
Relying on the physical organs to achieve illumination,
sight, hearing, smell, and taste each have their respective supports;
yet thought and consciousness ultimately depend upon the organ of the mind.
It is like a person who possesses a residence: the eastern pavilion extends hospitality to the worthy,
the southern balcony draws in the light,
and the northern window invites the breeze.
The western window reflects the moon;
the master sits upright in the center of the hall to gather the functions of the four senses.
This is as the Tathāgata’s discourse explains: the mouth, nose, ears, and eyes each have their own presiding deity.
If one eye becomes diseased, the visual faculty is immediately impaired;
both eyes would then necessarily become blind.
If one ear becomes diseased, the auditory faculty is immediately injured.
Both ears ought to have become deaf;
yet now it is not so.
From this we know that the spirit uses the body as its vessel, rather than being identical to the body itself.
It is further said:
"The mind is the root of deliberation; deliberation cannot be lodged in other parts.
If it were located in the mouth, eyes, ears, or nose," [it would not be the mind].
This argument is correct;
however, it would not hold if it were applied to the minds of others.
Although the ears and nose share this same physical substance, [the principle remains distinct].
They cannot be mixed together,
because those they oversee do not share the same vessel;
the vessels and utensils used by each are distinct.
Although his mind resides within that physical form, its manifestations can interpenetrate,
because the divine principle is equally subtle and his consciousness and deliberation are identical in their efficacy.
Thus, the Book says:
"Open your mind and moisten my own.
As the *Shijing* says:
"Others have their own hearts..."
I have reflected upon this:
Duke Huan of Qi relied on the strategies of Guan Zhong,
and the Founder of Han employed the counsels of Zhang Liang.
All of these are fundamentally rooted in one's own form and are merely entrusted to another's portion.
Why then say that the feelings of Zhang Jia cannot be deposited in the body of Wang Yi?
Can the nature of Li Bing not be entrusted to the body of Zhao Ding?
A question was asked:
"The physical form of a sage is just like the physical form of an ordinary person."
Yet there exists the distinction between the ordinary and the sage;
thus we know that the body and the spirit are distinct.
He replied:
It is not so. That which is refined gold can reflect light;
that which is defiled cannot.
How could the refined gold that is capable of reflecting have any impure substance that it does not reflect?
Furthermore, how could the spirit of a sage ever be lodged within the vessel of an ordinary person?
Furthermore, there is no spirit of an ordinary person who merely inhabits the body of a sage;
thus, the countenance of Xun and Hua possessed eight-colored eyebrows and double pupils.
The dragon-like countenance and horse-like mouth of Xuangao represent the extraordinary nature of his physical form; likewise,
the seven apertures aligned upon the heart of Bi Gan signify the peculiarity of his internal constitution.
"The gallbladder of Boyue was as large as a fist;
this is a distinction of the physical organ of the mind.
Therefore, the sages categorized him as always different from ordinary beings."
It is not only that the Way transforms all living beings,
but its form also transcends all phenomena.
Since the essence of ordinary beings and sages is identical, I dare not rest complacent.
Question: You say that the physical form of a sage must necessarily differ from that of an ordinary person.
I venture to ask:
Yang Huo resembled Zhongni,
and Xiang Ye bore a resemblance to Emperor Shun.
Shun, Xiang, Kong, and Yang possessed wisdom that transformed their outward forms; how is this so?
The answer is:
Ming resembles jade but is not jade;
the jū bird belongs to the class of the phoenix but is not a phoenix.
Such things truly exist.
It is only natural for humans to be thus.
Xiang Yang’s appearance was that of a man of integrity, yet he was not in reality;
because his inner faculties were uneven, his outward appearance was of no benefit.
Question: It may be that ordinary people and sages differ, as their physical forms and capacities are not uniform.
However, since the sages have reached the ultimate limit of reality, there can be no duality in principle; yet they still possess diverse appearances. Why is this?
That the spirit is not bound by physical appearance is made even clearer by this fact.
He replied:
The sages are identical with the Sage;
they share the same vessel as the Sage, yet their vessels need not be identical.
It is like horses of different coats that are equally swift.
Jade differs in color yet is equally beautiful;
thus, the "Jinji" and "Chuhe" gems were valued equally as being worth an entire city.
Likewise, the "Lin-lou" and "Dao-li" steeds both reach a distance of a thousand li.
Question:
We have already heard that form and spirit are not two distinct entities;
therefore, it stands to reason that when the form perishes, the spirit must also be extinguished.
I venture to ask:
the Classics state,
"One establishes ancestral temples for them so that they may receive offerings as spirits."
"What does this mean?
He replied,
"Such is the teaching of the sages."
Thus, by following the heart of the filial son,
one restrains the tendency toward negligence and meanness;
it is through this that one brings the Way to spiritual depth and clarity.
This is what is meant by that.
A question was asked:
"Bo You appeared wearing armor, and Peng Sheng manifested as a boar."
The works of the Five Classics record these matters;
could it be that they merely establish a teaching?
The answer is: No.
"Monsters are vast and indistinct; some exist while others perish. Those who die by reason are numerous, yet not all become ghosts.
Why then should Peng Sheng and Bo He alone be able to do so?
Appearing now as humans and now as pigs."
He was not necessarily a prince of Qi or Zheng.
Someone asked:

Today, alone receiving the imperial decree of the Liang dynasty, he carries the Way so that the myriad beings may be extricated from their delusions;
his virtue and longevity cause the nine provinces to exalt his illumination.

For a hundred years, he has impartially sustained and gathered [beings];
for a thousand ages, he has subdued all laboring men and moving creatures.
The Dharma Master’s wisdom is profound and resolute.
In upholding [the teachings], all were in full accord;
his resolve was pervasive, penetrating, and agile.

Lü Xù bows with reverence.

Regarding the profound mystery of the Way of the Spirits: it is vast and obscure. It is not something that can be fully grasped through the limited scope of human intellect. Thus, although the teachings of the Buddha have been transmitted for over four hundred years, their true essence remains difficult to fathom. Consequently, those who practice them often deviate from the correct path. This is because the Way of the Spirits is subtle and hidden; its manifestations are not easily perceived. Therefore, when the sages established the rites, they did not rely solely on the written word, but rather sought to manifest the truth through the medium of concrete forms. Now, as for the śramaṇas: they are those who have renounced worldly life to seek the Way. They shave their heads and wear coarse robes not out of a desire for appearance, but to signify their departure from the mundane. They abstain from grain and consume only medicinal herbs not out of a desire for asceticism, but to cultivate the spirit and nourish the mind. They dwell in mountain forests and remote valleys not out of a desire for seclusion, but to distance themselves from the clamor of the world. They observe the precepts and maintain purity not out of a desire for personal merit, but to serve as a model for the common people. However, in recent times, many have abandoned the true intent of these practices. Some have become entangled in secular affairs, while others have neglected their spiritual cultivation. If such individuals are not examined and selected, the integrity of the Sangha will decline, and the influence of the Buddhist teaching upon the state will diminish. Therefore, I propose that we establish a standard for the selection of monks based on their actual conduct and realization, so that those who truly embody the Way may flourish, while those who merely wear the robes without substance may be distinguished and corrected. This would ensure that the Way of the Spirits remains pure and that the benefits of the teaching continue to support the governance of the realm. The masses of people harbor compassion and obey Heaven’s decree not to kill;
how much less would they harm pigs or sheep and drink their blood?
By this reasoning, it may be inferred.
That they are not spirits is because the true deities of the Five Peaks are manifestations of the vital essence (*jing*); above,
they emulate the celestial pivot (*xuánjī*), and below, they sustain heaven and earth (*qiānkūn*).
Inheriting the Way, it is pure and void, without sound or resonance;
one does not rejoice in honoring it,
nor does one grieve in treating it with contempt.
Whether praised by thousands or reviled by ten thousands, the spirit neither increases nor diminishes.
Yet you falsely claim and feign authority, stirring the vital energies of the living through empty pretenses;

To violate this brings calamity;
such flattery and hypocrisy in every advance and retreat leave no trace of the path of the worthy,
and result only in the disparagement and humiliation of the True Divinity.
This is not the way.
Therefore, the Huangluozi jing (Scripture of the Yellow Robe Master) and the Xuanchong ji (Records of the Mysterious Center) state:
"Those who claim to be deities of mountains and peaks are invariably pythons."
Those who claim to be deities of rivers and seas must be turtles, crocodiles, fish, or tortoises;
those who claim to be deities of Heaven and Earth or parents must be cats, wildcats, or other wild beasts;
and those who claim to be deities of generals must be bears, brown bears, tigers, or leopards.
Those who claim to be the deities of officials must be monkeys or apes;
those who claim to be the deities of dwellings must be dogs, sheep, pigs, or calves;
and those of gates, doors, wells, stoves, and broken vessels are likewise such creatures.
Ghosts and demons assume false forms and are all called "spirits," striking terror into the myriad people;
this is the influence of licentious ghosts.
All of these are recorded in the scriptures;
they are clear evidences transmitted [through tradition].
Since your demonic portents gradually began more than six years ago.
He summoned those from the four quarters, and there were none who did not respond;

If those with heavy karma pass away first, you will simply say their "reckoning has ended.

Brandishing my halberd and brandishing my bright sword, I can shatter mountains;

Proclamation to Mara (by Shi Zhijing). (14) Proclamation to Mara by Shi Zhijing. Shi Zhijing. Shi Zhijing.
I prostrate myself again and again at the feet of General Ming.
Though we share different landing places on the profound path, humanity and heaven form a single unity;
although our respective teachers differ, the three realms are one and the same.
Every time I planned a virtuous assembly to express my long-accumulated devotion,
the underlying principles remained obscure, which was why we were kept apart.
Now, the Dharma King governs the world, and all ten directions yearn to follow him.
The divine net is now being spread, its cords and meshes further tightened.
The time for the Great Penetration approaches, and the great assembly is near.
Unable to bear the longing of my thoughts, I have written this letter merely to convey my sentiments.
Now, when times are obstructed there must be a way through, and when misfortune ends, there comes prosperity.
A thousand sages have followed one another, and a multitude of teachers have succeeded each other.
Long ago, our Imperial Ancestor, the Sovereign Heavenly King, embodied the transformative process and responded to the auspicious signs; he rose like a dragon from the primal realm.
Relying on the form of sovereign power to bring the myriad states into alignment,
and brandishing the blade of benevolence to cover the six realms;
his majesty sweeps away the four evils and clears the three worlds of existence.
He was now about to uphold the grand framework across the eight regions and cast the divine net throughout the universe,
bringing tranquility to the seven wildernesses and peace to the nine lands.
Yet, while the profound essence does not lament, the true countenance remains serene and still;
though the layered brilliance continues to shed its luster, it is like an empty boat overturned upon the waves.
Thus, it causes the perverse like ants to rise in succession and the predatory like owls to erupt in violence.
The true path has been obscured by defilement, and the dust of delusion has clouded the assembly of the pure.
Cruelty has descended upon the masses of living beings, and its poison flows through ten thousand kalpas.
Sentient beings who cherish the Way, though diverse in mind, share a common indignation.
I, the Dharma King, have inherited the Mandate and responded to the destiny of the age to bring order to chaos.

Grasping the Celestial Banner, I encompass the three thousandfold world system.
Holding the sacred charts, he magnified the Great Enterprise;

He pacified and comforted the common people and skillfully settled the officials;
he encouraged and guided the sentiments of the masses and consoled those who were afflicted.
Wisdom and strictness were held firmly within his breast.
He donned divine armor upon his body;
he took pity on the innocence of the eighteen realms and lamented that the path of the three emptinesses was severed.
His resolve was to rectify the vast wilderness and surely pacify manifold calamities;
throughout the hundreds of regions and thousands of states, all bowed high to his transformative influence.
Yet Your Majesty, harboring no suspicion, allowed yourself to be doubly deluded and self-subverted.
Because they deeply harbor the sentiments of the ignorant, they cling to false views;
like wolves seizing the heavens of desire and owls hooting at the divine palaces,
they cause rebellion and disintegration on the borders, resisting and obstructing the sacred mission.
It is said that one may ascend to a great station and reform grand regulations;
having perused these two or three [points], I have consequently sighed.
In the past, when the Great Universal One governed the world, all quarters of the realm submitted like shadows following forms.
There was a deceitful and deluded heavenly demon who did not observe the proper seasonal rites;
he disturbed the Sage’s hearing and troubled the Divine mind,
leading his troops to block the void.
Strategic forms undergo ten thousand transformations;
polished armor reflects the morning sun as frost-edged spears sweep across the realm.
Divine drums vyingly rise in resonance, their echoes surging beyond the four quarters.
They strode with arrogance and swaggered about, deeming themselves powerful and flourishing;
yet when the royal army once stirred, the host of evils was utterly destroyed.
The multitude who had been lost in delusion changed their hearts, prostrating themselves at the mere sight of the wind and shadow of the imperial might.
How much more so for you, who lead a mere handful of fierce warriors without any organized host, unable even to form a proper army;
yet you wish to rebel against and oppress the Chinese capital,
usurp the sacred authority, and transcend the Most Victorious One.
I consider myself to have been unworthy; could this not be true?
Now that Śākyamuni governs the world, the Way flourishes more than in previous kalpas.
Sublime transformations spread vast and far-reaching, as divine nets command from afar;

His strategic acumen was that of an Arhat, and his extraordinary schemes were transcendent.
Therefore, he commissioned Satata— Holder of the Seal of Authority, Former General of the Vanguard, Commander-in-Chief of Jambudvīpa, and Marquis of Guīyì—

The divine spirit towers as high as Mount Sumeru, his fierce vigor enshrouding the world.

Leading a host of hundreds of billions, he soared like a phoenix upon the celestial highway.

His brilliant nature reflects radiant light, and his golden countenance shines afar;
