The General Who Holds the Censorate’s Seal, Great General of the Stabilizing Domain, Supreme Commander of the Nine Heavens, King of the Eight Abodes, Vimalakīrti:
his extraordinary calculations are inconceivable, and the standard of his Dharma extends far and wide;
his person embodies divine grace, and his skillful means exceed ten thousand transformations.
When he breathed, the nine provinces followed like clouds;
when he uttered a shout, the ten directions bowed like grass before the wind.
He took pity on those lowly people, who were innocent and suffering in bitter anguish.
Leading a multitude of nine hundred billion, he drinks his horse at the ford of emptiness.

He is the Commander-in-Chief with Sealed Authority, the Great General Who Surveys the Rear, the Overseer of the Military Affairs of the Thirteen Heavenly Capitals, the King of the Nine Abodes, and the Great Mañjuśrī.
Inheriting the distant origin, his form illuminates the three realms;
descending from the Purple Palace, his spirit is lofty and his substance vast.
He responds appropriately to a thousand paths, with profound calculations numbering in the tens of thousands.
The myriad movements of all beings are felt within a single body;
the manifold anxieties of the world are stilled in a single thought-moment.
Deeply embracing compassion, his conduct encompasses the four means of integration.
Leading a multitude as vast as dust motes, he soars through this land:

the General Who Maintains the Command and Rectifies the Teaching, the Grand Marshal Who Records the Affairs of the Mara-Subduing Army, the Colonel of the Multitude of Wickedness, the Middle Thousand-King Avalokiteśvara.
His wisdom and strategy were profound and deep, and the branch of his insight reached far and wide.
He was clear-sighted and versatile, penetratingly discerning the three firm foundations.
At times, he concealed his traces among the heterodox to manifest his extraordinary edge as it rose up.
Sometimes he employs expedient forms to bring relief from the suffering of those submerged in mire and scorched by fire;
a wave of his hand shatters the Iron Ring Mountains,
and a breath from his mouth causes the floating clouds to crumble like precipitous cliffs.
He is the uninvited friend of the myriad regions.
Leading the multitudes without thought for himself, he brandishes his halberd like a tiger’s roar.
He is the Great General Who Spreads Transformation with Invested Authority, the Supreme Overseer of the Three Realms, the Crown Prince, the Greatly Compassionate Maitreya.
His wondrous substance transcends the net of the heavens, and his innate brilliance stands preeminent.
His body surpasses diamond in hardness, and his mind dwells beyond the realm of dust.
His fierce spirit pierces the clouds, and the branch of his wisdom strikes far and wide.
The non-arising [of phenomena] revolves within his breast;
expedient wisdom responds beyond the realm of worldly affairs.
His aspirations are directed toward a specific aim, and there is nowhere he goes that he does not succeed.
He exercised both majesty and benevolence, establishing both the ultimate and conventional truths;
leading eighty-four thousand followers, he maintained rigorous vigilance while awaiting his command,
as brave warriors overflowed the great trichiliocosm.
The Vajra-warriors fill the eight directions;
all contemplate assisting in the expedition to roll up the six realms under their banner.
They mount the precious chariot of the various *pāramitās*.
He guards the cultivated path of the Eightfold Right Path;
he mounts the spiritual horse of the Six Supernatural Powers;
he holds the divine reins of the profound source of emptiness.
He bends the powerful bow of the four *dhyānas* and releases the sharp arrows of expedient insight;
his war-horses neigh with vigor, and his light steps move with noble grace.
Having served the imperial court with never-failing devotion,
five hundred noble masters and disciples, perceiving the divine mandate through their profound insight,
have come to submit to Your Majesty’s transformation of the world.
The Sage Sovereign opened his breast to receive their sincerity and moved by their spirit, granted them submission;
he bestowed upon them names and ranks, conferred fiefs and rewards, and granted them territories.
Their merit equaled that of the veteran ministers, and their fame covered the myriad realms.
Yet what kind of mind do you harbor, harboring perverse schemes and lingering haughtily on the remote frontiers to plot for the security of your eternal position?
Your poisonous harm breaks forth upon the masses,
and your calamities flow through eternal kalpas.
How lamentable! How erroneous!
In the past, Your Majesty was deluded by external things due to the exigencies of the times.
Your mind was deranged and deluded; you threw yourself into danger and fled abroad.

Though a single transgression among a hundred deeds may cause even the wise and eminent to lose their way for a long time, we hope that you will awaken to this, turn back from folly, and acknowledge your guilt.
May you present yourself before the Imperial Gate (Xiangwei), withdraw your hairpins, and join in the company of the eminent scholars.
One should use the Way to bring joy to oneself and ensure that one's reputation remains intact from beginning to end.
How can one instead harbor the ignorant, cling to errors, and seek a precarious sense of security in a false position,
relying on the mountain of delusion to elevate oneself?
They rely on the forest of views for their recreation and rest;
they indulge in the defilements of the six desires and take pleasure in perverse delusions to gratify their natures.
They raise the lofty banner of arrogance and lead the fierce armies of ignorance;
striding boldly upon the desolate paths, they recklessly toy with the sacred vessels of state.
To usurp the celestial palace and rival the sun and moon—
fear that this shall not be achieved;
yet with a single raised hand, one can obscure the three luminaries.
To attempt to fill the great ocean with soil is a task difficult to accomplish,
even when one merely directs the mind toward it as a mere conceptual goal;
yet the General’s cultivation of merit at the profound ford has been sustained from a most remote origin.
His countenance is radiant, drawing the eyes of all;
the foundation for his downfall is easily ascended,
and the merit he has long cultivated is truly lamentable.
You may return there to cultivate future relations, turning back in submission to apologize for your transgressions at the Red Gate.
By harmonizing your bonds through the Way, both your family and state will survive;
you and your ministers shall be equally illustrious, and your lives and reputations will find peace.
With his vision clear and his perspective far-reaching, his retinue remains tranquil;
how beautiful this is!
Now that the royal army has triumphantly set forth, the ten directions raise their bridles in eager anticipation.
Holding aloft the *dharmadhātu* banner, they lead the host of holy sages;
the Way-staff shines as the vanguard,
while the divine drum resounds in the rear ranks.
At the first strike of the divine bell, the ten directions collapse;
the ocean waves fly in spray and the dry lands surge with boiling heat. At that moment—
Mount Sumeru is contained within a single speck of dust;
heaven and earth revolve upon a single chariot;
the Immovable One rests peacefully within the left lapel of one's garment.
The wondrous and joyful radiance shines from his right hand;
since his supernatural power is such as this,
how could it be withstood?
I, the Dharma King, embodying the Way and possessing benevolence and compassion, could not bear to launch an immediate attack.
I have temporarily halted all my armies and briefly reined in the spirit-steed.
As I approach the border, I dispatch this letter in the hope of turning back your deluded chariot.
You should quickly establish a sound plan to surrender with your hands bound and return to the capital.
Entrust your life to the imperial court and roam at ease within the profound realm;
let your illustrious name shine from within while your physical form dwells externally.
In the highest position, who else but you could rightfully hold the reign?
Now, kindness lies in recognizing the subtle shifts of fortune, and wisdom values avoiding calamity;
it is through understanding one's limits that one knows when to turn back.
What the superior man prizes is precisely this:
the high autumn for transforming calamity and the excellent season for securing merit.
In ancient times, King Jie of Xia was unrighteous and the King of Yin launched a punitive expedition against him;
Zhou Wu established his army against Shang Zhou who had headed the rebellion.
This is the divining mirror for all ages and the clear admonition for generals.
Although we may have diverged from one another in our conduct during our youth,
our refined elegance ought to be as one in the flavor of the Way.
Amidst the rugged difficulties of the human and celestial realms, what is there to cause such separation?
Upon reading it, my thoughts suddenly became clear, and I understood its intent.
It is for this reason that I feel a private sorrow over the phrasing of your previous letter;
I do not wish for the fragrance of the orchid to wither in summer, nor for the long branches and fine tips to be broken.
Reflect deeply on these words and carefully calculate for yourself;
do not allow your person to fall into the three evil realms like grain tumbling from a winnowing basket.
Do not allow the six heavens to grow only tares and weeds.
As I gaze upon the emerging ears of grain, my heart is filled with apprehension.
On the verge of this journey, I send this letter; my feelings are deeply troubled.
The words do not depend on the meaning. 57.

On this day when the five turbidities boil over and human life spans appear at one hundred years, I, the Subject Vajragarbha—King of the Tenth Stage, General Who Subdues Māras, Imperial Protector of Jingzhou, and Commander-in-Chief with Authority over All Military Affairs of the World-System as Numerous as the Sands of the Ganges—[declare: (Note: The text fragment provided ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)

Prostrations and salutations above.
To the Ministers of the Sagely Court:
We respectfully submit that the six realms of existence are illuminated by the mirror of the sun.
The myriad streams flow back to the king of the hundred valleys;
the ten thousand transformations are unified in the void and the profound.

while phenomena lack a convergence of divergent tendencies;
therefore, the Tathāgata emerged in solitary majesty, transcending the profound darkness of ignorance.
He has diligently cultivated merit throughout vast eons,
illuminating the lofty heights of the three evil realms and uprooting profound ignorance from its very inception.

he surveyed the pivotal mechanisms of the transformation of all things.

as for his outstanding and preeminent spirit and his radiant, blazing divine light,

The body manifests in ten thousand different forms yet is not manifold;
its essence accords with the ultimate subtlety yet is not singular.

Responding to the myriad stimuli without weariness,
encompassing the ten thousand movements while remaining eternally still,
traversing as many worlds as grains of sand in the Ganges in the blink of an eye.
He pacified the eight wildernesses in an instant;
yet the two polarities remained collapsed and could not be leveled,
and his physical strength shifted in secret without being diminished.
Inhaling great fires without being scorched;
embracing vast floods without being drowned.

it encompasses the six directions of the universe,
yet its vastness cannot be fully described.
Subtly entering the Uninterrupted [Samādhi], it cannot be described as small;
therein, it nurtures and transforms all things within the azure heavens, encompassing the functions of the primordial mother.
It is without desire and without action, yet there is nothing it does not do.
Soaring upon the path of adaptive response,
they wander at ease beyond the realm of existence and non-existence,
reaching the pinnacle of all the sages.
Tranquility and serenity are the realm of Nirvana;
those of the Two Vehicles conceal their thoughts within the state of profound oblivion,
while those of the Ten Abodes suspend their reflections at the pivot of movement and stillness.
The Brahma King sighed in admiration and turned to him for refuge;
Śakra, having submitted his heart, grew weary of his station.

This too has reached its ultimate limit.

Emerging from the five realms of existence, he arose like a dragon;

As a King of the Way over the three worlds, his virtue pervades the ten directions.
Throughout the imperial domains as vast as the sands of the Ganges and across the great trichiliocosm,
he lay within the secluded chambers of the nine meditative concentrations and ascended the cloud-palace of the seven factors of enlightenment.
They bathe in the pure pool of the eight liberations and roam the vast gardens of dhāraṇī;
thus they dwell in the palace of compassion.
Seated upon a throne of universal emptiness,
he possesses the manifold excellences of a celestial official with the crown-mark (uṣṇīṣa),
flanked on his left by Maitreya and his like.
On the right, he is the peer of Mañjuśrī;

The Postscript to the *Hongming lun* (Treatise on Propagating and Clarifying [Buddhism]). Compiled by Shi Sengyou. That which I have collected as the *Hongming lun* serves as a defense for the Dharma against insults.
The elegant discourses of the erudite and the subtle expositions of the eminent serve as the vanguard for crushing heterodoxy and shattering delusion,
and as the defensive moat for propagating the Way and protecting the Dharma.
This has already been fully prepared.
Nevertheless, the wise do not become deluded;
those who are deluded deviate from wisdom.
If one guides them with the profound Dharma, they ultimately fail to grasp it;
therefore, I have again extracted passages from secular classics to provide concrete evidence for the point.
These words do not concern mere ornamental flourish, but rather return to the principle of essential reality.
It is intended so that those who have strayed onto mistaken paths may return before it is too late, thereby resolving all doubts in their entirety;
thus it is called the *Hongming* (Propagation and Clarification).
As the treatise states:
Now, the distinction between the two truths differentiates the monastic from the secular.
The Way’s Dharma is empty and quiescent,
encompassing the three realms through impartial contemplation.
The teachings of the mundane world are narrow and stagnant;
they cling to a single state to limit the mind.
When the mind is limited to a single state, everything beyond the reach of one's ears and eyes becomes a source of doubt.
When one contemplates the three realms as equal, the principle of spiritual transformation constantly shines forth;
yet it is because sentient beings cling to doubt and thus lose sight of this radiance that they remain forever submerged in the cycle of existence.
Upon careful examination, secular teachings all take the Five Classics as their model.
Those whom we revere are only the heavens; those whose teachings we follow are only the sages.
Yet, one cannot fathom the forms of the heavens nor peer into the minds of the sages;
thus, though we honor and believe in them, [we remain in ignorance].
If one is already dim-sighted and lacks clarity regarding this,
how much more so when the Buddha is more venerable than heaven and his Dharma is more subtle than the sages—
manifesting his transformation throughout the realm?
The principle is severed from the realm of bondage;
even Jianwu was struck with awe and terror at the Milky Way.
How could worldly people not feel doubt and alarm before the ocean of awakening?
Once they were startled into awakening, they were as amazed as if they had encountered the Milky Way;
first, they doubted that the scriptural teachings were far-fetched and grand yet lacked evidence;
second, they doubted that death meant the extinction of the spirit and that the three periods of time did not exist.
Third, the doubt that one cannot see the true Buddha and that this would be of no benefit to the governance of the state.
Fourth, the doubt that there were no teachings of the Dharma in antiquity and that it appeared only recently during the Han era.
Fifth, the doubt that the teachings originate from barbarian regions and thus their transformation is not suited to Chinese customs.
Sixth, I suspect that while the Dharma was obscure during the Han and Wei dynasties, it only began to flourish during the Jin era.
Because of these six doubts, the tree of faith has not yet been established;
since those about to drown must be rescued, I have thus compared and discussed them.
If one suspects that the scriptural teachings are迂誕 (obscure and extravagant) and grand yet lack evidence,
it is because the accumulation of kalpas is inexhaustible and the worlds are boundless.
In this world, everyone knows that beyond a hundred years, there must be ten thousand years.
Yet they do not believe that ten thousand accumulated transformations extend to vast kalpas;
this is to limit the mind in measuring the workings of creation.
All know that beyond the realm of China (Chixian), there must be the four extremities of the world.
To lack faith that there are further worlds beyond this active realm is to employ a biased view to judge the Great Void.
Formerly, Tang asked Qi He:
"Are there limits to the eight directions, above and below?

Within the inexhaustible, there is yet further inexhaustibility;
it is for this reason that I know it to be infinite and endless.
The great sages of antiquity relied upon principle to instruct the sagely, and their teachings have remained in accord with the scriptures like a seal meeting its impression for a thousand years.

For with a heart the size of a square inch, they plot for their own persons and yet fall into error;

If one suspects that when a person dies, the spirit is extinguished and the three periods of time do not exist;
